item.title: The best Linux distro for you probably isn't the one everyone recommends
item.itunes:title: The best Linux distro for you probably isn't the one everyone recommends
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Making the switch from Windows to Linux comes with a lot of challenges for first-time users, and it actually starts before you even use Linux for the first time. The biggest question you'll be asking yourself is what distro to install, and you'll likely turn to the internet for help.

But watching a YouTube video or reading an article about the best Linux distros comes with a few caveats. The most popular recommendations aren't always going to be what's best for you, so the best place to start is actually with your own hardware.

The best, but for who?

Broad advice can be a problem

There are plenty of Linux distros you'll see recommended for a first-timer, and the reasoning behind those recommendations usually comes from familiarity or general ease of use. Ubuntu is one of the first to be brought up, both because it has the backing of a huge organization and a long history, but also a desktop environment that many consider more approachable than most alternatives, and even Windows itself.

Others might recommend Fedora if you prefer faster updates and want an official release that use the KDE desktop, which is much more similar to that of Windows. You might even see Linux Mint, which is a little more grounded and offers a familiar and relatively lightweight experience.

New to Linux? Here are 7 of the best beginner-friendly distros for you to try

Get up and running with Linux in no time.

32
By  Rich Edmonds

These are all great distros and they have a lot to offer, so their popularity is completely justified, but the videos and articles making these recommendations also aim to have mass appeal, so the recommendations don't really take into account your specific hardware. Ubuntu may be great, but as of the latest release, it requires at least 6GB of RAM, so if you're trying to play around with an old PC, it won't be for you. And even others that might run on your system could end up being pretty slow.

How old is your PC?

The best distros may not be for you

Ubuntu, Fedora, or more configurable distros like Arch Linux are great and have a ton of features. And with something like Arch, it's a fairly lightweight system to start with, so you might think any old PC can run it. But the problem with many of the most popular distros is that they also get updated frequently and tend to adapt to newer hardware as it comes out, in detriment of older machines.

If you're starting with a computer that's over ten years old, you need to first look for options that are lighter on resources. Linux Mint may still be a good option in this context, but depending on specific configurations, you may want to try different options. The default Mint comes with the Cinnamon desktop, but there's a variant that comes with Xfce, a more antiquated and lighter desktop that may be more suited for your PC. It may not look as nice, but it will run more smoothly and still get frequent updates.

But if you keep going back to PCs over 15 years old, you might have to resort to options that are truly more obscure. Projects like MX Linux and antiX exist with the specific purpose of extending the life of very old and low-end PCs, and those may be better for you. Start by checking how old your PC is, and go from there. It's best to ask for specific advice once you have your PC's specs at hand.

Windows left this old laptop to rot, but Linux brought it back to life

If this thing can run, your laptop can too

1
By  João Carrasqueira

The opposite can also be true, though. A distro like Ubuntu won't always have the latest Linux kernel by default, and newer versions can offer compatibility with recently-released hardware. If you have a brand-new laptop and you want Linux on it, you might want to opt for something like Fedora or Arch Linux, where kernel updates tend to be available very quickly and enable better support for new hardware.

What kind of device is it?

Desktops, tablets, and handhelds are all different

Another factor you need to consider when picking a Linux distro is the type of device you're dealing with. Say you have something like a Surface Pro tablet and you want to put Linux on it. Sure, any Linux distro will run, but this is a tablet, and most Linux desktops don't work very well with tablets. GNOME does try, but the experience is still far from ideal.

Thankfully, there are desktops that are more designed for tablet use, too. One of the most notable efforts is Plasma Mobile, a variant of KDE Plasma designed for touchscreen devices, which you can get through a distro like the official Fedora KDE Plasma Mobile spin, Debian, or even Arch.

Alternatively, say you have a gaming handheld like the Asus ROG Xbox Ally and you heard that Linux is better than Windows because of the Steam Deck. That may be true, but the Steam Deck specifically comes with SteamOS, and that distro is why it works so well. That said, there are alternatives like Bazzite or CachyOS that offer dedicated gaming handheld releases with the same benefits as SteamOS, but you shouldn't rush into installing Ubuntu or Arch just because they're Linux. You have to pick the right option for your form factor.

For all their differences, standard laptops and desktops do behave mostly the same, so a distro that's good for one is good for the other. It's mostly touchscreens and gaming controls you want to be more careful with.

I replaced Windows on my gaming handheld a year ago, and the industry caught up to me

Linux gaming has too much momentum for hardware vendors to ignore

By  Joe Rice-Jones

General advice only goes so far

Whether it's a YouTube video or any kind of broad recommendation, you have to remember that the majority of the audience for content on the internet has relatively modern devices, and those recommendations are usually made to have broad appeal. It's not as simple as searching for "best Linux distro" and choosing the first one or the most popular one, because your hardware may not always play nice with those options.

item.title: I segmented my smart home network and broke everything until I fixed these three settings
item.itunes:title: I segmented my smart home network and broke everything until I fixed these three settings
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Once your smart home starts to grow and you have dozens of cheap smart plugs, cameras, and other devices, you might decide to create a dedicated IoT VLAN to keep all of this separate from your primary PCs and maintain network security.

However, as soon as you do this, you'll probably begin to notice issues, including Google Nest speakers or AirPlay receivers being unable to connect to your phone, and your home system integration discovery freezing. This is likely because you haven't accounted for multicast and link-local boundaries, aggressive IGMP snooping switches, and Wi-Fi access point client isolation.

VLANs only segment layer 2 broadcast domains. They don't natively forward any zero-configuration discovery protocols. Understanding how mDNS repeaters, reflectors, IGMP queriers, and wireless multicast-to-unicast conversion work is the missing link for running an ultra-secure, isolated IoT VLAN without breaking all your smart home devices. All it takes is adjusting a few quick settings.

Your smart home needs to be able to communicate

Don't choke your devices

When you have a range of smart home devices, they communicate through protocols like Apple HomeKit, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Philips Hue, and Matter, which rely on mDNS broadcasting over UDP port 5353 to the IPv4 or IPv6 multicast group. This means that if you want to connect to these devices from your phone, PC, or other devices that aren't on your IoT VLAN, you might struggle.

By design, mDNS packets are crafted with a Time-to-Live (TTL) of 1. This means that the moment an mDNS packet hits a router interface and crosses from VLAN 20, your IoT VLAN, to VLAN 10, your trusted VLAN, the router decrements the TTL to 0. As a result, the packet is completely dropped, so your phone on VLAN 10 literally never receives the broadcast announcing that the speaker or smart TV exists whatsoever.

When it comes to security, this can be great at preventing hackers from accessing your trusted devices, but when it comes to actually using your smart home as intended, it can cause errors. The fix is in the form of an mDNS repeater or reflector. Enabling a true mDNS repeater, which rewrites TTL and reads broadcasts on specific interfaces, can solve 80% of missing device discovery without opening any firewall holes.

You can do this by using UniFi: go to Settings > Networks > Global Network Settings, and you should find the Multicast DNS option. You can toggle this on.

3 hidden Android Auto settings I always change to make every drive so much better

The in-car platform's Developer Settings include several useful features for regular Android Auto users

By  Patrick O'Rourke

IGMP Snooping might be your respite

Those with managed switches should tweak this setting

Another issue you might be facing is IGMP snooping and missing multicast queries. When you're setting up an IoT VLAN in order to prevent multicast streams from flooding every single Ethernet port like ancient broadcast hubs, your smart managed switch might enable IGMP snooping. The switch listens for IGMP 'join' messages from clients and then decides which ports should receive the multicast traffic.

This can lead to issues if your network doesn't have an active IGMP querier, which is a designated router or core switch polling the network periodically to ask, "Who wants this multicast group?" The switch's membership table expires after just a few minutes, so devices will connect fine initially, but minutes later, casting, and local control silently stop working until the switch is rebooted.

To rectify this issue, you need to calibrate your IGMP snooping and Querier. Check your managed switch's settings for IGMP snooping and ensure it's enabled. However, make sure you designate your core gateway as the Querier IP if it's not already.

Access point settings cause issues too

Multi-cast enhancement is the fix here

A common issue with IoT-specific networks is actually access point settings as well. This can be as a result of client isolation and multicast enhancement. When you're setting up a guest network, many routers and access points have an isolate station or client isolation toggle on for IoT SSIDs. This prevents Wi-Fi devices from communicating with other Wi-Fi devices on the same access point radio. This can break local hub-to-bulb communication or just any smart device from actually being able to chat.

Multicast rate limiting/enhancement is another pressure point, because unoptimized Wi-Fi access points can drop low-speed multicast frames to conserve wireless airtime. This means that it can drop device discovery beacons before they ever reach the wired switch, enabling IGMP v3 snooping and multicast-to-unicast conversion on your access point. This ensures discovery packets are reliably delivered to a mobile phone over Wi-Fi. This means that your phone can actually see the smart home devices that you have.

You can do this by opening your IoT Wi-Fi profile and checking the settings. You should disable client isolation and then enable multicast enhancement. Next, set a stable minimum 2.4 GHz beacon rate (usually 6Mbps or 12Mbps is best).

You can keep your network safe

While also ensuring it is usable

Building a segmented smart home isn't about slapping firewall drop rules on everything and hoping for the best. Of course, you want your network to be secure, but this shouldn't come at the expense of it actually working correctly. Consumer smart home protocols were essentially invented for flat dumb home networks.

Making them work inside an enterprise VLAN architecture requires respecting multi-cost physics. Luckily, you don't have to get rid of your VLANs altogether. Instead, tweak some of your settings, including your mDNS repeater, configure your IGMP querier, tune your Wi-Fi multi-cost settings, you should be able to rectify the problem.

item.itunes:summary:
Default apps on Android phones have a bad reputation for being mediocre attempts at fulfilling the core demands of usersr. Ever since I bought my first Android smartphone, I have been neglecting almost all the default apps because they have mundane designs, limited feature sets, excessive tracking, and numerous promotions. These apps never improve or build upon their original features and don't fix their shortcomings.

Samsung tried to update its default apps, but they are nowhere near the experience some third-party apps offer. Unlike in the old days, I actually use a few of the default apps on my current phone, but third-party apps still rule. If you cannot bear with the default apps on your phone, have a look at some options that I use.

VLC is the best media player

Samsung Video Player needs refinements

I have had quite a bad experience with default video players. The biggest gripe was copying videos to the phone and then trying to play them with the built-in video player, only to discover that it didn’t support the format. It was always hit-or-miss with multiple video players, including some third-party ones. But VLC never faced this problem and has been playing my media files, videos from family functions, vacations, and other sources without any problem.

Its interface has witnessed a few subtle facelifts over time, but the app looks more or less the same. I’m more concerned with the video playback than its looks, and the app never disappoints in that department. Anime takes up a big chunk of my daily screen time, and viewing it at 2x playback speed is no problem for VLC. Some video files tend to struggle on my old Xiaomi phone, but that’s a hardware limitation and not a software one.

4 launchers that turn my boring Pixel home screen into something actually useful

Give your Pixel a fresh look with these powerful launchers.

By  Yash Patel

Samsung’s Video Player has a few necessary features, including subtitles, sync, and playback speed adjustment, yet it cannot match VLC’s quality. The native player struggles with diverse video formats, can add subtitles, but lacks a download feature, and limits playback speed adjustments to 2x. VLC has a subtitle download feature, can swap audio tracks, and lets me set timers, adjust the equalizer, play it as an audio file, and speed up the video to 8x. It’s hard to find so many features in a free, zero-ad Android app.

SMS Organizer keeps messaging simple

Google Messages is an eyesore

Google tries to squeeze in as many apps as it can with each OEM because it owns the OS. Its messaging app is the default on my Samsung phone, and I used it in the initial phase, when it didn't require an online account. But as it became more pushy and downright stopped me from accessing the app until I signed in with a Google account, I decided to find something better.

On my previous phone, I loved using the SMS Organizer app made by Microsoft. The main reason for choosing it was that it had categories for automatically sorting messages. The promotional material could stay in one category and general messages in another, while the banking category would show my transactions. There's even a finance section to track your bank account balance via incoming transaction messages. I haven't really felt the need for more features and barely miss what Google Messages offers.

I turned my old phone into a device that does something my $300 smart home gadgets can't

Turns out I haven't been utilizing my old phone enough.

1
By  Anurag Singh

SMS Organizer shows OTPs in bold whenever they arrive, and Microsoft even fixed the notification system, making it a complete package. Apart from that, it's a truly offline app if you prefer it that way, and that was enough reason for me to run away from Google Messages. The sad part is that Microsoft is calling it quits on this exceptional messaging app, and while they've not disclosed a date, it will retire in the future. I'll continue to use it until then while keeping an eye out for something similar.

Niagara Launcher makes the home screen likable

One UI Home feels distracting

Samsung’s One UI Home starts to feel bleak and distracting after a point. First, it's a basic home screen like you get with any other Android OEM, with a bunch of icons and widgets scattered across one or more pages, and a side-scrolling app browsing section. It's slightly better at customization, but it's not a home screen you can bear for long. I switched to Niagara Launcher shortly after purchasing a Samsung phone three years ago. However, it wasn't my first encounter with Niagara Launcher.

I installed Niagara Launcher in 2020 and continued using it until I switched to a new phone. My main reason for returning to it was a minimalist-style launcher with a vertical app list and useful customization options. After installation, you have to pick a favorite app to pin on the home page, and that's about it. The home page and the app list blend into one page, and accessing the app list feels faster than before. There are no widgets in the default setup, but you can add them if you want.

I turned my Samsung Galaxy into a speed machine by ditching Samsung's bloated launcher

The official launcher is of no good.

1
By  Anurag Singh

I also like the Quick Reply feature that helps me to revert to a message without opening the app. It's a custom way to open a reply interface on a portion of the home screen, where you can send your message and be done with it. Niagara Launcher also offers better themes and customization options, along with a few extra features, such as summaries. I use the free version because it meets my needs, and I have a custom button on the home screen to lock it without pressing the power button.

Bitwarden stores my passwords

No more Google Password Manager

I host a custom Vaultwarden server on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2W, which uses Tailscale to serve it over HTTPS and enables remote access. My concern about this is data privacy. I briefly used LastPass before switching to Google Password Manager, then to a self-hosted alternative. Vaultwarden uses the official Bitwarden app to meet phone-version needs, and there's no problem with it. I hadn't set up HTTPS until recently, and without it, the app wouldn't work at all.

Tailscale helped me serve Vaultwarden over HTTPS, and that opened doors for the app. Like any other password manager app, Bitwarden offers autofill, custom vaults, a password generator, and a few more options. Now, my passwords stay on the Raspberry Pi and are backed up to an external SSD as well, helping to ditch Google’s cloud storage dependence for password storage.

Switch to better apps

Native apps are mostly lackluster on Android phones, and Samsung apps are no different. However, there are some exceptions, like the Samsung Browser, which is the default app and better than Chrome. Its file manager app, called My Files, is also good, but I prefer the above-mentioned ones over Samsung's other solutions. SMS Organizer and Bitwarden are two underrated ones that you might not have tried before.

Niagara Launcher

Niagara Launcher is a minimalist Android home screen with plenty of customization options.

item.title: I built my first PC almost 20 years ago, and these 4 blunders prove I didn't know what I was doing
item.itunes:title: I built my first PC almost 20 years ago, and these 4 blunders prove I didn't know what I was doing
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My first brush with PC building happened nearly 20 years ago in 2007. It had been seven years since I had gotten my first PC, an HP pre-built with an Intel Pentium III processor. It was time to upgrade to something faster, and, hence, my first custom build was powered by Intel's Core 2 Duo chip (the E7300, if I remember correctly).

The excitement of building and enjoying a new PC was enough for me to ignore nearly everything else that goes into the setup. Optimizing BIOS settings, partitioning the hard drive, and overclocking the CPU were some of the things I was absolutely clueless about back then. I must have spent years leaving performance on the table before I realized my mistakes.

5 terrible PC components I used for years that I shudder thinking about now

If I had known better, I wouldn't have touched them with a ten-foot pole

19
By  Tanveer Singh

Picking the wrong RAM slots

It all started in the build phase

Today, installing two DIMMs in slots A2 and B2 is second nature, but two decades ago, I probably installed my RAM sticks in whichever slots looked best. I wasn't aware of the impact of installing the RAM in the incorrect slots, and since the PC didn't show any obvious errors, I never revisited the issue, leaving dual-channel performance on the table.

If only I had checked the motherboard manual, the recommended A1-B1 or A2-B2 combination would have been clear. Most likely, I was using DDR2 RAM, but the performance loss of using single-channel memory was still there. I remember reinstalling the RAM only a few years later, when I finally realized my mistake. This wasn't a BIOS or Windows setting, but rather a simple mistake that became a blunder in terms of real-world impact.

Your PC might be running single-channel RAM right now, and the performance hit is bigger than you think

Single channel can literally halve your performance

By  Ty Sherback

Using the default fan curves for years

My PC was cooked, and I didn't even know

We all know that the pre-configured fan curves in the BIOS aren't the best, but I didn't know that back then. My newly built PC was booting and functioning well, and the fans were spinning. Whether they were too loud or too slow, I accepted either scenario as in-spec behavior. I didn't know that I could mess around with my CPU or case fans, and tune them to my liking.

BIOS capabilities twenty years ago may not be what they are now, but Windows utilities like SpeedFan still allowed significant control over fan behavior. My CPU probably lost a significant amount of performance to overheating, and it could have been avoided simply by changing some points on a graph.

5 reasons why you should set custom fan curves in BIOS

Allow your motherboard to control your fan speeds.

By  Rich Edmonds

Creating a single partition

It works now, but it wasn't a good idea back then

You probably know that multiple drive partitions aren't needed anymore, but until just a few years ago, it was common practice to have at least one partition in addition to the main system partition. This wasn't just blind conformism either; having additional partitions protected you from data loss if you needed to reformat your OS.

I remember reinstalling the OS on my Windows XP system on more than one occasion, and extra partitions would have helped me a lot. Whether it was oversight or superstition that prevented me from partitioning the drive better, I can't say. My C: drive went through many reincarnations, so more partitions would have given it a longer life.

You don't need to reinstall Windows, use these built-in tools instead

Is a clean install your go-to for stubborn Windows issues? Think again. There are ample recovery options right at your fingertips.

5
By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

Staying away from CPU overclocking

I missed out on a major performance boost

  • Credit: Flickr
  • Credit: Flickr
  • Credit: Flickr
  • Credit: Flickr

The Core 2 Duo era was one of the golden periods of CPU overclocking, with 50–60% frequency boosts being easily achievable on air cooling. These chips had made the jump from 65nm to 45nm (shocking, I know), so users could force higher clocks without the need to amp up the voltage too much. This was legitimately a massive and free performance boost available simply by tweaking the BIOS.

Since I stayed away from the BIOS for a few years after building my first PC, overclocking seemed like too big a task. I preferred the safety of stock settings to the hassle and unpredictability of overclocking. Messing with the frequency and voltage of my CPU was unthinkable, so I mentally put overclocking in the "don't touch" bucket.

Your motherboard's default settings are tuned for stability, not speed

Honestly, I wouldn’t want it any other way.

By  Hamlin Rozario

The first few years of my PC journey weren't the best

I'm not proud of missing out on settings and best practices that would have been obvious to many other users. I was just venturing into custom PC building, and gravitated toward safe defaults instead of maxed-out performance. My next build was drastically different, and I had learned a lot more by then, but I still wish I was an enthuiast in the mid-2000s.

It was time to upgrade to something faster, and, hence, my first custom build was powered by Intel's Core 2 Duo chip (the E7300, if I remember correctly).

The excitement of building and enjoying a new PC was enough for me to ignore nearly everything else that goes into the setup. Optimizing BIOS settings, partitioning the hard drive, and overclocking the CPU were some of the things I was absolutely clueless about back then. I must have spent years leaving performance on the table before I realized my mistakes.

If I had known better, I wouldn't have touched them with a ten-foot pole

By  Tanveer Singh

It all started in the build phase

If only I had checked the motherboard manual, the recommended A1-B1 or A2-B2 combination would have been clear. Most likely, I was using DDR2 RAM, but the performance loss of using single-channel memory was still there. I remember reinstalling the RAM only a few years later, when I finally realized my mistake. Single channel can literally halve your performance

My PC was cooked, and I didn't even know

5 reasons why you should set custom fan curves in BIOS

Allow your motherboard to control your fan speeds.

item.title: I thought all 4K Blu-rays were created equal until I learned about this key difference
item.itunes:title: I thought all 4K Blu-rays were created equal until I learned about this key difference
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you see a black case and the 4K Ultra HD badge, you likely assume that every title delivers the absolute pinnacle of 3840x2160 pin-sharp visual fidelity. However, for a lot of movies, whether that's major modern superhero blockbusters or even early 2010s action movies, your 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray might look surprisingly soft, noisy, and pretty close to a standard 1080p Blu-ray. This is down to a key technical reality: not all 4K Blu-rays are actually native 4K.

The industry is flooded with 2K upscaling, DNR-scrubbed transfers, and compressed BD-66 disc authoring masquerading under the same premium label. The 4K UHD badge on a retail box indicates the disc container's output resolution, not the master's provenance. Understanding the difference between native 4K scans and 2K upscaled masters, along with disc-layer bit-rate budgets and HDR color volume, is key to curating a true reference-grade physical media collection.

The difference between 4K native and 2K upscales

Not all 4K is the same 4K

There is a major difference between 4K native movies and 2K upscales, also known as fake 4K. This is down to the post-production CGI bottleneck. Even when movies are shot on 6.5K-8K digital cameras or 35mm-17mm film, the captured raw footage is ingested into a digital intermediate, or DI, pipeline for visual effects, compositing, color grading, and editing. Because rendering CGI at true 4K is exponentially more expensive and time-consuming for VFX houses working under tight studio deadlines, many 2000s to 2020s CGI-heavy blockbusters were mastered and finalized at 2K resolution.

2K is 2048 x 1080 in terms of pixels, which is a major difference from 4K. That means that, after this is done, the studios have to upscale. When studios author the 4K Blu-ray, they take that 2K master and apply algorithmic upscaling to scale the canvas to 3840x2160. This means you're paying for an uncompressed 4K container that contains a glorified 1080p or 2K image with added high-frequency sharpening and artificial grain.

These differences are super noticeable in older movies like 2001: A Space Odyssey, Alien, or Lawrence of Arabia. These films frequently look far sharper than modern $250 million blockbusters because a physical 35mm film has an optical resolving power of roughly 4K to 6K, while 70mm reaches 8K to 12K. A fresh 4K photodiode scan of the original camera negative yields genuine native detail.

4K Blu-ray already has a successor, and it isn't what I expected

A 200TB experimental optical disc could dwarf 4K Blu-ray, but data centers and archival storage will likely benefit first.

24
By  Jeff Butts

Disc bitrates need to be considered.

You don't want compressed footage

Another factor that plays into whether your 4K UHD disc is actually true 4K is disc authoring and bitrate budgets. There's a difference between BD-66 and BD-100. BD-66 is dual-layer and holds up to 66GB of data, with max sustained transfer bit rates of around 72-92Mbps. BD-100 is a triple-layer drive that holds up to 100GB and delivers transfer speeds that burst past 100Mbps to 128Mbps.

This leads studios to cut costs and use compression crushing to save on disc-pressing manufacturing costs. Studios often cram a 2.5-hour movie with multiple lossless Dolby Atmos audio tracks and language dubs onto a cheaper BD66 disc. To make it fit, authoring houses aggressively compress the video bitrate down from 45Mbps to 55Mbps, introducing macroblocking in complex action scenes, smoke, and shadow gradients. A proper BD2001 GVC encoder has the headroom to maintain an uncompressed 85-100+ Mbps master stream without compression artifacts.

You can spot a real 4K disc before purchasing with a variety of different tools. The first are Blu-ray.com and Caps-a-holic databases. You can check the user and reviewer master breakdowns before buying; these are specifically tagged as Video: native 4K and Video: upscaled 2K. You can use the screenshot comparison sliders on Caps-a-holic to inspect the true pixel-level resolution. Another thing to consider is the disc layer inspection. You can verify whether the physical release is pressed on a BD-100 or BD-66 disc by checking the technical specifications metadata on the back of the case or in fan database entries.

2K upscaled discs aren't all bad

Other elements save the day

Luckily, just because a 4K UHD disc you might have invested in isn't true 4K doesn't mean it's a complete write-off. There is a silver lining here: thanks to HDR and WCG, they essentially save the day even on 2K discs. This is because resolution is only half the battle.

The true leap in visual fidelity on 4K discs is often high dynamic range (HDR), whether that's HDR10, Dolby Vision, or HDR10+, as well as a wide color gamut like DCI-P3 or BT.2020. You get a much larger, expanded dynamic contrast. Even if a movie is an upscaled 2K DI, like Mad Max: Fury Road or Avengers: Endgame, it benefits from 10-bit color depth, spectacular highlight pops like sun reflections, explosions, and laser blasts hitting 1,000+ nits, and deep, unclipped near-black shadow detail.

Alongside the image quality, there is also lossless audio inclusion. 4K discs almost universally mandate the highest-tier uncompressed audio mastering in the form of Dolby TrueHD with Atmos or DTS-HD Master Audio that blows compressed streaming audio tracks out of the water.

Physical media looks better, but Plex gives me the one thing discs never could

Blu-ray has the best quality, but my Plex library is convenient and looks great

9
By  Tanveer Singh

Physical media is the best

But you should prioritize true 4K

Physical media remains the undisputed king when it comes to home cinema. However, the retail industry treats 4K as a marketing bullet rather than a technical guarantee. Just because the disc you're buying isn't true 4K doesn't mean you should completely overlook it.

However, it's worth double-checking the digital intermediate provenance, looking for BD-100 pressings, and prioritizing those to ensure your home theater setup is fed the true reference-quality masters it was built to display.

item.title: I ditched my CoreXY 3D printer plans for a bedslinger, and my build volume doubled for half the price
item.itunes:title: I ditched my CoreXY 3D printer plans for a bedslinger, and my build volume doubled for half the price
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been in and out of the 3D printing hobby for a decade, and the market has changed dramatically in the years since. Recently, when I was looking up options for a new 3D printer, my biggest dilemma was picking between a standard bedslinger and a fully enclosed CoreXY machine. My pick? The all-new Bambu Lab A2L.

I picked the device for a fairly straightforward reason. I wanted the ability to print big objects without spending significantly more money or opting for a much more complicated machine. The fact is, a CoreXY machine is considered the natural upgrade path. The fixed bed, faster movement and better handling of tall prints are legitimate reasons. But unless I blow the bank, it doesn't solve my biggest complaint -- a small build plate.

5 things to consider before buying a 3D printer

Consider these important factors before making a big investment

2
By  Sammy Ekaran

The bigger build volume is a real advantage

A bed slinger is good enough for my use case

A CoreXY printer comes with obvious mechanical advantages. The bed only moves vertically while the toolhead handles the X and Y movement. That's useful with tall or heavy prints because they aren't constantly being tossed around backwards and forwards. But that doesn't mean that everything is rosy. A bedslinger is mechanically simpler, and it can often accommodate a larger build volume at a lower price.

The Bambu Lab A2L immediately stood out to me for its massive build volume. Clocking in at 330 x 320 x 325mm, that's effectively twice the volume of the A1 that I had previously rejected. It's also a significantly bigger build volume than any CoreXY printer you can get at a similar price point.

For me, that build volume is the feature that made the decision for me.

If I'm buying a 3D printer to solve practical problems, it needs to be large enough to print practical solutions. My desk is full of little problems that are just easier to solve with a 3D printer. I've been making brackets, mounts, trays, organizers and Gridfinity components. A large build volume means that I can one-shot these prints without factoring in joints, alignment issues and assembly.

A 330-mm wide build plate means that I can make things that simply wouldn't fit on a smaller machine. Just today I printed an oversized dinosaur prop for my nephew that would have to be split in 3 parts on a smaller machine. Elsewhere, I already need 4 build plates for each drawer in my Gridfinity setup, a smaller machine would mean as many as 8. That's more time spent printing, and more alignment and joints to figure out.

And, yes, technically a moving bed is not as elegant as just moving the print head. However, technology has come a long way. I wasn't expecting much, but whatever magic Bambu Lab has done with its adaptive vibration compensation to control the effects of the moving platform does the trick. All that to say that the printer is plenty fast, not that I'm trying to win benchmarks here.

It goes without saying that there are some limitations to an open-bed printer that can't be worked around. You're not going to be printing ABS, ASA or other engineering material on this printer. But for a hobbyist like me, that's a non-issue. I suspect it'll not be an issue for a lot of people. With standard PLA, PETG and TPU, the printer performs swimmingly.

The A2L's biggest advantage is value

More build volume for the money

There's another reason why the A2L's design in particular, and opting for a bedslinger in general, makes a lot of sense. That's cost.

The A2L starts at around $469. Even when you factor in the cost of an AMS Lite, which is an optional, but in my opinion a non-negotiable extra, you clearly come out on top. The value proposition is very different here compared to standard models like the A1, and premium fully-enclosed CoreXY machines. For many (including yours truly), the money going towards a larger build volume makes sense.

An enclosed printer with a rigid frame sounds great until it simply can't fit the objects that I want to print. The A2L makes the right compromises. Bambu Lab has put engineering resources into the one thing that matters every single day — the ability to print an enormous print, think helmets and cosplay parts, on a single build plate.

In my workflow, between the time savings and the literal cost savings, the A2L is cheaper to run than a smaller printer no matter how I look at it.

Compatibility with the AMS Lite system further shifts the equation in the A2L's favor. A large build volume and the ability to print in multiple colors at this price point is, honestly, a game changer.

The right balance of specifications

CoreXY is, on paper, obviously a superior system. But that's not the point of this article. Unless you're printing professionally, a machine that strikes the right balance and feature set makes most sense. Features like automatic bed levelling, flow calibration, vibration compensation, and a built-in camera for keeping tabs on an ongoing print have effectively turned the printer into an appliance. And that's amazing as, for all practical purposes, you can send a print job from your phone and pick it up once you get the notification telling you that it is ready.

There's value in turning the 3D printing hobby into something so accessible that anyone can pick it up, while also building a product that is actually useful for building practical parts. All that, at an accessible price point. The Bambu Lab A2L doesn't necessarily prove that bedslingers are better than CoreXY printers. Technically, they are not. But this balance of technology, volume and price might make it an incredible choice for most hobbyists. It certainly has been for me.

item.title: This note-taking app is refreshingly boring, and that makes it special
item.itunes:title: This note-taking app is refreshingly boring, and that makes it special
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I love exploring different apps and software, especially when I come across something that takes a different approach from the tools I normally use. Over time, I've noticed that many note-taking apps keep adding features until they start to feel like complete productivity platforms.

That made me curious about simpler alternatives. While looking for lightweight apps for everyday use, I came across Notally, a note-taking app with a much more focused approach. It immediately caught my attention because it doesn't seem interested in doing everything. I decided to give it a proper try and see how well it works for writing something down without turning it into a whole productivity task.

What is Notally?

It makes writing feel refreshingly simple

Notally is a minimalist note-taking app made for Android users who want a simple place to write things down. The moment I start a new note, I get a clean space to put my thoughts down. There is no pressure to organize everything perfectly or decide where an idea belongs before I write it.

That simplicity has become the biggest reason I keep coming back to it. When an idea pops into my head, I can quickly type it out and move on. It feels more like grabbing a piece of paper than opening another productivity tool.

I also like that Notally doesn't make every writing session feel important. Some notes are just quick thoughts, rough ideas, or things I don't want to forget. They don't need a complicated workspace. For me, that's where Notally works best. I can open it, write what I need, and close it when I'm done.

5 self-hosted markdown editors that sync without the cloud

Powerful markdown, private sync, pure control

2
By  Yash Patel

Features that make my note-taking productive

The little things that save time

Once I started using Notally regularly, I noticed that its simple design doesn't mean it lacks useful tools. The features are practical, and I can use them without changing the way I normally take notes.

I particularly like the different ways I can organize my notes. I can use colors and labels to separate different types of information, while pinned notes keep important things within easy reach. Search also makes it much quicker to find an older note. I can archive notes I don't need right away without deleting them.

Notally also lets me add images to my notes, including JPG, PNG, and WEBP files. I can create lists and checklists, set reminders, and even adjust the text size when I want something easier to read. Rich-text options such as bold, italics, monospace, and strikethrough are useful when I need a little more formatting.

I also like the light and dark themes, as well as the home-screen widgets for quick access. The app feels fast when I'm opening notes or typing, which is important when I'm trying to capture something quickly. When I need to move my writing elsewhere, Notally lets me export notes as PDF, TXT, JSON, or HTML. It also supports clickable phone numbers, email addresses, and web links.

There are plenty of features here, but they don't feel like they are competing for my attention. They make the app more useful when I need them.

It isn't for everyone

And that's exactly what makes it better

After using Notally for a while, I can see that some people will want more from their note-taking app. If I needed real-time collaboration, shared workspaces, advanced project management, or deep integrations with other services, I would probably choose a different tool. Notally makes more sense for individual use. It works well when I'm managing my own notes and don't need other people involved in the process.

That's an important distinction because no single note-taking app works for everyone. Some people want an app packed with connected services and advanced workflows. Others want something they can use on their own without building their entire workflow around it.

I think Notally knows where it fits. It doesn't try to compete with every type of productivity software, and that makes the choice easier for me. If my requirements are straightforward, I don't need an app designed for a much bigger job.

This open-source app does what Google Keep refuses to do, and the difference is exactly what I needed

A privacy-friendly note app that feels refreshingly simple.

1
By  Yash Patel

A note-taking app that knows its place

Notally changed my view of what I actually need from a note-taking app. I don't need every note to become part of a larger system, and I don't need an app to turn simple writing into a productivity routine. I just need something that handles everyday notes reliably.

That makes Notally a good fit for a specific kind of user. If you mainly write down ideas, lists, reminders, or short pieces of information on Android, it covers the basics without getting in the way. It won't replace a full writing or productivity platform, but it doesn't need to.

Notally

Notally is a minimalistic note-taking app with a beautiful material design and powerful features.

item.title: This router setting reduced my Wi-Fi speed, but it's the best change I've made to my network
item.itunes:title: This router setting reduced my Wi-Fi speed, but it's the best change I've made to my network
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We instinctively chase the biggest numbers when it comes to performance, whether it's PC hardware or networking. That's probably why your router's default channel width is greater than what it should be, so that performance looks good in a speed test. While a higher channel width directly translates to more bandwidth and speed, the overall result might not be what you want.

I experienced this myself when I experimented with different channel width values in my router's settings. Dropping to a lower value reduced my maximum Wi-Fi speed in some areas of the house, but the connection improved in every way that mattered. Apps and websites became snappier, buffering was minimal, and the Wi-Fi range improved tangibly.

Your Wi-Fi slows down every evening, and your ISP has nothing to do with it

With Wi-Fi activity peaking all around you, your connection naturally suffers

By  Tanveer Singh

Your router's default channel width is probably suboptimal

Bigger isn't always better

Users on Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 are more familiar with 160 MHz channels, and even 320 MHz channels on the latter. That said, even those on Wi-Fi 6 can make use of wider channels on the faster 5 GHz band by tweaking their router settings. Your 5 GHz band is probably set to use wider, 80 MHz channels to offer the maximum bandwidth possible in your plan.

This results in a bigger number when you run a speed test, since the bigger slice of the spectrum allows the router to push more throughput. This should improve performance, but in real-world conditions, it rarely helps. This is because most of us live in densely populated urban environments, where your neighbors' Wi-Fi competes with your own on the same spectrum.

The greater the channel width, the greater the interference with nearby Wi-Fi networks. Once your router combines multiple channels into a single wider channel, it increases the signal-to-noise ratio. At longer distances, your router faces greater packet loss, making the problem worse. Using 80 MHz on your 5 GHz band probably shows a better speed test, but it tanks your actual Wi-Fi performance.

You might be making your Wi-Fi worse by blindly choosing the widest channel on your router

Wider channels promise higher bandwidth, but also introduce more interference

By  Tanveer Singh

Lowering the channel width can tangibly improve Wi-Fi performance

I experienced it myself

Recently, I was checking out my router's admin page to see if I could enable DFS channels. While that wasn't an option on my router, I spotted that the 5 GHz band was set to 80 MHz channel width. I probably picked it a while ago, hoping to boost the speed in the furthest rooms of the house.

I changed it to 40 MHz, just to see if it would make a significant difference. And I'm glad I did that, since my 5 GHz performance became genuinely smoother. The overall bandwidth dropped slightly, but the connection was way snappier and more reliable. The random slowdowns when watching YouTube on my TV or browsing Instagram on my phone were gone. Even the range improved when I moved to the rooms away from the router.

This is because a lower channel width reduces co-channel interference with neighboring networks. Your router is less likely to occupy the same slice of spectrum as other routers. It also allows your router to avoid DFS channels, which can force a lengthy re-scan if the router detects a weather or airport radar signal. Hence, the chances of a connection drop are reduced, too.

Your router's 5 GHz band has hidden channels that are faster than those you're probably using

DFS channels could offer congestion-free 5 GHz performance

By  Tanveer Singh

Use a free utility to find the best wireless channel

Don't ignore channel selection

  • Credit: NetSpot
  • Credit: NetSpot

While you're tweaking router settings, it's recommended to revisit the channel you're using. Your router's automatic channel selection picks a less-crowded channel on every reboot. However, if you rarely reboot your router, your channel selection is most likely outdated. The channel scan your router performs is a static snapshot, not a dynamic scan that updates the "best" channel periodically.

Hence, it's recommended to manually choose a clean wireless channel by using a utility like WiFi Analyzer. It will show you the number of networks on every band and channel, along with the signal strength of each network. You can choose the channel with the least number of strong networks.

Optimizing channel selection alongside channel width will have a greater impact on your Wi-Fi performance. You'll minimize interference and actually enjoy a stable connection instead of chasing vanity metrics.

My router was doing 5 things that I never asked it to, and I wish I had changed them earlier

These router defaults should be changed as soon as possible

By  Tanveer Singh

Wi-Fi speed isn't everything, especially in crowded environments

Most people treat their Wi-Fi bandwidth as the north star for their Wi-Fi performance. In reality, a lot more goes into making a stable, reliable, and snappy connection. You need to minimize interference and latency, and maximize range before you can conclude that your connection is optimized. Reducing the channel width reduces co-channel interference and improves the range of your Wi-Fi.

item.itunes:summary:
Besides the graphics card, the CPU is the most exciting component of a build. Whether you're a gamer, power user, or professional, the CPU plays a pivotal role in your system. Many people, however, are still prone to believing some CPU myths that were busted a long time ago. Be it about the most important CPU specs, the dangers of modifying voltage and power settings, or the fear of bottlenecks, these myths might be keeping you from using your CPU to the fullest, or pushing you to overspend on the CPU.

7 myths about PC performance that are still surprisingly common

You might believe in some of these yourself

11
By  Tanveer Singh

CPU overclocking is dangerous

Outdated, maybe, but not really risky

Messing with your CPU's frequency, voltage, and power settings might sound risky, but it's nothing more than a simple hit-and-trial. Overclocking your CPU involves finding the right combination of settings that squeezes extra performance from your silicon without making everything unstable and keeping the spike in power consumption to a minimum. As long as you stick to one of the many CPU overclocking guides on the internet, the risk of taking things too far is negligible.

The worst that can happen is your system shutting down due to an unstable overclock, post which you can just revert to less aggressive settings. Overclocking will not damage your CPU or reduce its lifespan to any significant degree, as long as you have adequate cooling hardware to keep things comfortable. Most CPUs these days don't have a lot to gain from overclocking; factory settings and automated boost algorithms already run the chips at near-100%. Still, if you want to experiment with overclocking, you can do so without worrying about killing your CPU.

6 ways you're guilty of reducing your CPU's lifespan

Simple mistakes that might be killing your CPU

22
By  Tanveer Singh

Undervolting reduces CPU performance

On the contrary...

Unlike overclocking, undervolting your CPU is focused on reducing temperature and power consumption instead of maximizing performance. However, a neat little bonus of the process is that your CPU can actually perform better with an undervolt. This works because undervolting reduces the voltage and, thereby, the heat dissipated by the processor. Lower temperatures mean the CPU can maintain boost clocks for longer, improving overall performance.

You stand to benefit from not just higher 1% low FPS, but also average FPS in gaming. By modifying the voltage-frequency curve for your CPU, you effectively allow it to deliver the same performance at a lower voltage and power level. The mileage will obviously vary for different users, but assuming that undervolting will always reduce performance is outright false. Many people regularly undervolt their CPU, and enjoy a performant, cool, and silent system.

4 mistakes people make while undervolting their CPU or GPU

You can't just lower the voltage and expect your desired results

4
By  Hamlin Rozario

Air coolers can't handle modern CPUs

You'd be surprised

Despite overwhelming evidence in favor of air coolers, many PC builders choose liquid coolers out of habit, believing air cooling just can't keep up with their power-hungry CPUs. While it's true that you absolutely need AIO coolers to tame top-tier chips like the Core i9-14900K, Core Ultra 9 285K, Core Ultra 7 265K, or Ryzen 9 9950X, most people aren't using these monsters. Modern 6-core and 8-core CPUs can be easily cooled with budget and mid-range air coolers.

Economical air coolers like the Thermalright Phantom Spirit 120 are renowned for their cooling performance. For less than $40, you can realistically cool almost all mainstream CPUs. And if you invest a bit more in a Noctua cooler, you could even manage to cool the highest-end processors. Unless you're overclocking a high-end CPU or running extreme workloads, you'll have no problem running an air cooler on your PC.

Thermalright Phantom Spirit 120 SE

Thermalright's Phantom Spirit 120 SE is a bigger version of its acclaimed Peerless Assassin 120 cooler. It has seven heatpipes compared to the six on the Peerless Assassin and is a bit bigger, which means better cooling capacity.

$36 at Amazon
Air coolers can handle almost everything, so who are AIO coolers really for?

Air coolers aren't the useless cousins of AIOs anymore, so why are liquid coolers still relevant?

By  Tanveer Singh

High CPU usage means a CPU bottleneck

Not always

A CPU bottleneck sounds scary to most people. After all, if your CPU is stopping your system, specifically the GPU, from achieving maximum performance, you'd be worried too. However, many users see unusually high CPU usage and incorrectly conclude that their CPU is bottlenecking their PC. While a CPU bottleneck is one possible explanation behind high CPU usage, it can't be looked at in isolation.

You might be playing CPU-demanding titles or gaming at 1080p, both of which can contribute to higher CPU usage than you'd usually expect. As the resolution increases, games become more GPU-bound, and you start seeing the load shift toward the graphics card. If you're noticing simultaneously high utilization of both the CPU and GPU, you might not have anything to worry about. Your system is well-matched, and is using the CPU and GPU to the fullest.

3 reasons for high CPU usage that aren't bottlenecks

High CPU usage alone doesn't mean you have a CPU bottleneck

4
By  Tanveer Singh

High-end gaming requires high-end CPUs

Law of diminishing returns

Pairing a high-end CPU with other high-end components sounds natural, but you don't need an expensive CPU for high-end gaming. If your graphics card and the overall system are capable of high-refresh-rate 1440p and 4K gaming, you don't really need to shell out the big bucks for a high-core-count CPU or one of the Ryzen X3D chips. At higher resolutions like 4K, you'll almost always be GPU-bound, and the CPU will become mostly irrelevant.

It's not that the CPU isn't important at 4K, especially when rendering the game at a lower resolution during upscaling. The difference between different CPUs, however, can be highlighted only when they're paired with the most powerful graphics cards. If you aren't using an RTX 5090 or RTX 5080, you'll struggle to see any major difference between, say, a Ryzen 5 7600X and Ryzen 7 9800X3D. This leaves most people with little incentive to invest in anything more than a 6-core chip for gaming.

Most of the myths I listed above aren't new, but they still persist in the minds of consumers. item.itunes:title: Proxmox's official Arm release doesn't support Raspberry Pi, so I installed it anyway
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When Proxmox announced official Arm64 support in Proxmox VE 9.2, the list of supported hardware made the intended audience clear. The first fully supported systems are the Nvidia Grace Hopper and Vera platforms, not the Raspberry Pi boards many of us already have sitting around the house. Proxmox explicitly states that device-tree-only single-board computers, such as the Raspberry Pi, aren’t supported, which would normally be enough to make me move on. Instead, it made me want to see how far I could get, because an official Arm build means the software finally exists, even if my hardware definitely wasn’t invited.

Proxmox releases full support for the Arm64 architecture, with a few key caveats

You can request access starting today.

By  Simon Batt

Proxmox finally treats Arm as a first-class architecture

This is much more than another community port project

Running Proxmox on Arm used to come with an immediate caveat. You could find community projects, unofficial repositories, and plenty of people willing to make it work, but none of that meant Proxmox itself supported what you were doing. Proxmox VE 9.2 changes that by making Arm64 an official second architecture alongside x86-64. It shares the same codebase, repositories, and release lifecycle, so Arm is now part of the product rather than something happening off to the side.

The rest of the stack is familiar, which matters more than I expected once I actually got into it. The Arm release is based on Debian 13.5 Trixie and ships the same versions of QEMU, LXC, and ZFS as the x86-64 release. Proxmox says the configuration, tooling, and documentation are essentially the same, aside from a few architecture-specific differences. I didn’t have to relearn Proxmox just because I’d moved to a different CPU architecture, and that makes experimenting with Arm much less annoying.

The official target is still much larger hardware than anything I had on my bench. Proxmox says the release was developed and hardened in collaboration with Nvidia and is already in production on supported Grace-based systems. It’s also working with other server vendors to expand the list of supported hardware. That’s enterprise territory, but for me, the important part is that Proxmox is now building and maintaining Arm packages itself instead of leaving that entire job to the community.

Getting it running on a Pi takes the manual route

There is no convenient Raspberry Pi installer waiting here

This isn’t one of those projects where you flash an image, boot it, and spend the next five minutes clicking through a familiar installer. Proxmox’s Arm requirements call for a host that boots via UEFI and exposes its hardware via ACPI, while the Raspberry Pi doesn’t fit that model. The route I followed starts with a fresh 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS Lite installation based on Trixie and adds Proxmox on top. That distinction matters because I wasn’t really installing a Raspberry Pi edition of Proxmox so much as making a Raspberry Pi OS installation acceptable enough for the Proxmox packages.

Most of the fiddling happens before those packages ever go on the system. The network configuration has to be changed to the setup Proxmox expects, including a Linux bridge, while removing NetworkManager and cloud-init.
